title: Hotspot Hunter: Sampling Strategies and Collector Matrix
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a compact, pragmatic guide for running lightweight profiling experiments and CI captures aimed at quickly finding CPU/latency hotspots in the serving runtime. It focuses on choosing the right sampler/collector for the question at hand, minimal local workflows, and CI artifact conventions so traces are searchable and useful for regressions.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: sampling-based captures (perf, pprof-like stacks, eBPF user-space probes, lightweight heap/alloc captures), collector selection matrix, quick CI job examples, artifact naming, short troubleshooting list.
- Non-goals: deep kernel debugging, full observability platform design, long-term retention/archival policy (ops will own retention).

Why a "light" approach:
We frequently need to verify that a change didn’t add a hot path or that a workload shift changed token latency distribution. Full end-to-end instrumentation is useful but slow. Lightweight sampling gives high signal with low cost: captures are quick, artifacts small, and they can be automated in PR/perf CI.

Collector selection matrix (quick reference):
- perf sampling (user-callchain): best for native C/C++ hotspots and JIT-ed code; low overhead for short tests; needs debug symbols to be fully useful. Good when suspecting kernel/user boundary or CPU-bound token generation.
- simple pprof-style (Go/Java): use runtime/pprof or async-profiler for Java; best for language runtime stacks, alloc hotspots.
- eBPF user-space probes (USDT / bpftrace): useful when you want to attach to specific tracepoints (e.g., kv cache hit/miss, batch enqueue/dequeue) with low overhead; excellent for correlation with syscall events.
- micro-sampler (periodic lightweight tracer): frequent short captures of stack tops (1–10ms) aggregated over minutes; good for intermittent spikes or skew.
- dynamic tracehooks (LD_PRELOAD / function-level): high signal but invasive; use only in local or dedicated test environments.

Tradeoffs (short):
- Overhead: perf < micro-sampler < eBPF probes (depends) < dynamic tracehooks
- Signal: dynamic hooks > eBPF probes > perf for inlined/JITted symbols
- Setup complexity: perf simplest on Linux; eBPF requires elevated privileges or kube DaemonSet and tuned CLAs

Local quickstart recipes:
1) CPU hotspot (native parts) with perf:
- Start server under realistic load (locally or in dev cluster).
- Identify PID: pid=$(pgrep -f redwood-runner)
- Capture 30s sample at 200Hz: sudo perf record -F 200 -g -p $pid -o /tmp/hotspot.perf.data -- sleep 30
- Convert to flame/stack report: sudo perf script -i /tmp/hotspot.perf.data | ./scripts/stackcollapse-perf.pl > /tmp/hotspot.folded
    && ./scripts/flamegraph.pl /tmp/hotspot.folded > /tmp/hotspot.svg
Notes: include binary and debuginfo in dev image or use addr2line to resolve addresses.

2) Short sampling for intermittent spikes (micro-sampler):
- Run a tiny script that uses async ptrace or sampling API to collect top-of-stack every 5ms for 60s. We store compressed stacks as gzipped ndjson for CI.
- Example minimal recorder (bash pseudocode):
  for i in $(seq 0 120); do stacktop_dump >> stacks.ndjson; sleep 0.5; done; gzip stacks.ndjson

3) eBPF-based collector for internal events (kv cache hit/miss):
- Use a prepared bpftrace or libbpf program in the tools repo. Attach to USDT probe emitted by runtime at send_batch() and cache_lookup(). Capture timestamps and pid/thread. Output condensed counters per 1s window.
- Keep probe payload minimal (counters + small tag) to avoid overhead.

CI integration pattern (perf-CI quick job):
- Job triggers: nightly perf job and optional on-large-PR (manually opt-in via label).
- Runner image: ubuntu-minimal + perf + addr2line + flamegraph scripts.
- Job steps (bash snippet):
  set -e
  export ARTIFACT_PREFIX="${GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER:-${CI_PIPELINE_ID}}-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"
  ./tools/loadtest.sh --scenario $SCENARIO --duration 60 &
  SERVER_PID=$!
  sleep 8   # warmup
  sudo perf record -F 250 -g -p $SERVER_PID -o /tmp/${ARTIFACT_PREFIX}.perf.data -- sleep 40
  sudo perf script -i /tmp/${ARTIFACT_PREFIX}.perf.data | ./scripts/stackcollapse-perf.pl > /tmp/${ARTIFACT_PREFIX}.folded
  ./scripts/flamegraph.pl /tmp/${ARTIFACT_PREFIX}.folded > /tmp/${ARTIFACT_PREFIX}.svg
  gzip /tmp/${ARTIFACT_PREFIX}.folded
  tar czf ${ARTIFACT_PREFIX}-prof.tar.gz /tmp/${ARTIFACT_PREFIX}.*
  # upload artifacts to CI with metadata labels: scenario, model, commit
Notes: keep perf capture short (30–60s); storing compressed folded stacks + svg keeps artifacts small.

Artifact naming and metadata (conventions):
- Name: <ci-id>-<scenario>-<model>-<arch>-<capture-type>.ext  Example: 1428-latency-smallgpt-a100-perf.tar.gz
- Metadata in artifact manifest (simple JSON file included in tar): {"commit": "<sha>", "scenario": "latency", "model": "smallgpt", "node": "a100-1", "start_ts": "ISO8601"}  (include as human-readable text file alongside binary artifacts)

Retention and storage guidelines (short):
- Keep CI artifacts for 14 days by default for PR jobs; nightly CI keep 90 days. Size target: < 50MB per job.
- If a perf capture > 100MB, store on long-term object store and reference it in the manifest.

Analysis checklist (what to look for quickly):
- Top recurring C frames that correlate with increased p99 latency.
- Heavy inlined callchains from commonly used allocator or memcpy patterns.
- System wakeups or I/O syscalls that increase when load increases.
- Sampling skew: check if signal is dominated by a single thread (e.g., GC or background IO).

Known anomalies and quick fixes:
- Flat stacks / lots of [unknown]: ensure debug symbols installed or use source-built images.
- Kernel noise spikes during captures: try isolating CPUs or use perf -e cycles:u to restrict to user time.
- eBPF permission errors in CI: run agent with CAP_BPF/CAP_SYS_ADMIN or deploy privileged DaemonSet on dedicated perf nodes.

When to escalate to deeper tracing:
- If sampling indicates blocking in runtime but callstacks unresolved, escalate to instrumented tracepoints (add logging/span in critical code path).
- For memory explosions or allocator source-of-truth use heap profilers (pprof/malloc hooks) rather than CPU sampling.

Quick primer: turning a CI artifact into a diagnostic ticket:
1) Capture: artifact tarball (folded stacks + svg + manifest).
2) Short summary: one-paragraph TL;DR (what changed, observed symptom, p50/p95 change, top-3 frames).
3) Attach artifacts and link to PR/commit.
4) Label ENG-RT PERF and assign to oncall or owning subteam.

Appendix: useful commands (copy/paste)
- perf top live: sudo perf top -F 200 -p $PID
- perf record & script: sudo perf record -F 250 -g -p $PID -o out.data -- sleep 45 && sudo perf script -i out.data | ./scripts/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded && ./scripts/flamegraph.pl out.folded > out.svg
- bpftrace one-liner (count cache hits by tid): sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_read /comm=="redwood-runner"/ { @[tid] = count(); }' -o cache_hits.txt  # replace probe with real USDT in prod

Open items and TODOs:
- Create a small in-repo Go binary that produces pprof-style stacks for quick captures (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/XXX).
- Provide a non-privileged eBPF capture path for CI (needs agent work).
- Define exact retention policy with SRE for perf artifacts older than 90 days.

If you use this doc: please add a short note with capture id and a quick conclusion so we can build an internal signal library of common root causes (e.g., "memcopy-regression-from-quantize-v2").

End.
